results.title: Do Sequential Recommendation Benchmarks Require Higher-Order Sequence Modelling? | Spotify Research

item.text: {"text":"Recent research supports history perturbation as a diagnostic of model reliance. [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduce a recency-bias metric and report that excessive recent-item emphasis can harm recommendation accuracy. [Scarcelli et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) search for minimal history edits that change sequential recommendations, providing a framework for ranking-sensitivity analysis. [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) find history-aware pairwise transition models outperform tested Transformers on four of five benchmarks. Their results motivate separating recency weighting and accumulated historical evidence from joint sequence encoding; they do not establish the same outcome on the four target Amazon categories.\n\nPractical probe design, inferred from these findings: mask recent windows, recurring-interest interactions, and isolated interactions; compare each with repeated random masks matched for interaction count, and match position where feasible when testing recurrence. Define recurring interests through observable item recurrence or title/description similarity, explicitly labeling semantic recurrence as a proxy. Evaluate chronological prefixes drawn only from training histories, measuring changes in next-item score, rank, and HR@10 alongside top-10 overlap and rank displacement. Keep candidates and the original unseen-item exclusion set fixed across perturbations. Compare position-preserving masking with deletion/repacking to expose positional artifacts. Stratify by history length and recurrence, then compare last-item, recency-weighted pooling, and sequence-encoder behavior. Greater sensitivity to an isolated latest purchase than to sustained recent interests would flag a modeling hypothesis for follow-up; perturbations measure model dependence, not causal user preferences or purchase effects."}
